title: The old World of Warcraft might be back, but my childhood isn’t
gist: Personal essay on Blizzard's re-release World of Warcraft: Forever, arguing that nostalgia has become a cornerstone of consumerism (eight of the decade's ten top-grossing films are sequels) and that restored multiplayer worlds are a new, more potent form of nostalgia monetisation aimed at now-ageing millennial players.

themes.theme: Nostalgia as a consumer business model

insights.claim: Exploitation of nostalgia has become a cornerstone of contemporary consumerism, with culture saturated by remakes, reboots and sequels of decades-old stories and characters.
insights.speaker: Max Moser
insights.so_what: IP-owning studios and publishers with deep back catalogues keep structural advantage over original-content bets.
insights.quote: the exploitation of “nostalgia” has become a cornerstone of contemporary consumerism

insights.claim: Of the 10 highest-grossing films of the 2020s so far, eight are sequels and the other two (The Odyssey and Barbie) are built on long-familiar cultural properties.
insights.speaker: Max Moser
insights.so_what: Box-office returns are concentrated in franchise IP; supports valuations of IP-heavy media owners.

insights.claim: Wicked's 20 uninterrupted years in London's West End have spawned two blockbuster films with further spinoffs likely, illustrating how a single property is mined across formats.
insights.speaker: Max Moser
insights.so_what: Cross-format franchise extension extends IP cash-flow lifetimes well beyond the original product.

insights.claim: The continued dominance of Marvel films suggests consumer appetite for returning to familiar fictional worlds may be effectively unlimited.
insights.speaker: Max Moser
insights.so_what: Argues against betting on franchise fatigue as a near-term theme.

themes.theme: Restored online game worlds as a new nostalgia product

insights.claim: Blizzard has released World of Warcraft: Forever, a legacy re-release of the original 2004 multiplayer game that lets players re-experience it as if newly launched, with new content woven into the familiar world.
insights.speaker: Max Moser
insights.so_what: Legacy-server re-releases are a low-cost way for game publishers to re-monetise old content to lapsed players.

insights.claim: Unlike films, multiplayer games are inhabited worlds with routines and relationships, so restoring a preserved game world is a uniquely powerful way to manipulate nostalgia, enabling thousands of players to regress collectively.
insights.speaker: Max Moser
insights.so_what: Social, persistent game IP may carry stronger nostalgia-driven re-engagement than passive media IP.
insights.quote: This restoration of preserved inhabitable worlds represents a unique development in our ability to manipulate nostalgia.

insights.speaker: Max Moser
insights.so_what: Ageing gamer demographics favour time-efficient game design and higher-spending, time-poor customers.

insights.speaker: Max Moser
insights.so_what: Legacy game content can recruit new generations, extending franchise lifetime value.

insights.claim: The author expects to keep chasing embellished childhood memories through the game despite knowing a true return is impossible, illustrating the durable but disappointment-prone demand nostalgia products rely on.
insights.speaker: Max Moser
insights.so_what: Nostalgia demand is repeatable even when consumers expect disappointment, supporting recurring re-release cycles.
insights.quote: Over the past two decades, I have returned to World of Warcraft more times than I care to admit on print.
